## Declarations and implementations

```plato
//==
// # Splines
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - Evaluating the Bezier splines
//  - Knot vectors and B-spline / NURBS domains
//  - Piecewise indexing and Hermite evaluation
//  - Evaluating the interpolating splines
//  - Deformation bodies for the control-point curves

library Splines
{
    //==
    // # Evaluating the Bezier splines
    //
    // Evaluation of the control-point curves declared in `splines.types.plato`.
    // De Casteljau's algorithm is the whole story: it is generic in `$T`, using it
    // only through Lerp, so one reduction serves points, vectors, and weights, and
    // the rational form is that same reduction run twice. Nothing from
    // `library Polynomials` is reimplemented here.

    //==
    // # Bezier curves of arbitrary degree
    //
    // https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Casteljau%27s_algorithm
    // De Casteljau's algorithm is the one Bezier evaluator that does not need a
    // closed form per degree: repeatedly replace the control values by the
    // lerps of adjacent pairs until one remains. It only needs Lerp, so it is
    // generic in the type variable `$T` and serves points, vectors, and
    // weights — and that genericity is now SPELLED, by the function's own
    // `where` clause (plato-393).

    // The de Casteljau reduction of a control polygon at t.
    // Precondition: xs is non-empty.
    //
    // Written ONCE, over `$T`. The body needs Lerp on a bare element, and the `where` clause is
    // what promises it: the element type of the array must be IInterpolatable, so the call is
    // licensed at the declaration, every call site is checked against the bound (an
    // `Array<String>` is rejected), and the emitted C# carries the matching constraint instead of
    // a throwing stub. Before plato-393 this was five hand-copied bodies — Point2D, Point3D,
    // Vector2D, Vector3D, Number — because a bound could only be inherited from a constructed type
    // in the signature, and the only one here is `Array<T>`, which is unbounded and must stay so.
    DeCasteljau(xs: Array<$T>, t: Number): $T where $T: IInterpolatable
        => xs.Count <= 1
           ? xs[0]
           : (xs.Count - 1).MapRange(i => xs[i].Lerp(xs[i + 1], t)).DeCasteljau(t);

    // The point on a Bezier curve of arbitrary degree at t.
    Eval(self: BezierCurve2D, t: Number): Point2D
        => self.ControlPoints.DeCasteljau(t);

    // The point on a Bezier curve of arbitrary degree at t.
    Eval(self: BezierCurve3D, t: Number): Point3D
        => self.ControlPoints.DeCasteljau(t);

    //==
    // # Rational Bezier curves
    //
    // https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zier_curve#Rational_B%C3%A9zier_curves
    // De Casteljau is linear in its control values, so running it on the
    // weighted points gives the numerator sum(B_i w_i P_i) and running it on
    // the weights alone gives the denominator sum(B_i w_i).

    // The point on a rational Bezier curve at t. Precondition: the weight sum
    // at t is non-zero.
    Eval(self: RationalBezierCurve2D, t: Number): Point2D
        => (self.ControlPoints.Count
                .MapRange(i => self.ControlPoints[i].PositionVector * self.Weights[i])
                .DeCasteljau(t)
            / self.Weights.DeCasteljau(t))
           .ToPoint;

    // The point on a rational Bezier curve at t. Precondition: the weight sum
    // at t is non-zero.
    Eval(self: RationalBezierCurve3D, t: Number): Point3D
        => (self.ControlPoints.Count
                .MapRange(i => self.ControlPoints[i].PositionVector * self.Weights[i])
                .DeCasteljau(t)
            / self.Weights.DeCasteljau(t))
           .ToPoint;

    //==
    // # Composite Bezier curves
    //
    // The canonical parameter is split evenly across the segments: segment i
    // covers [i / count, (i + 1) / count]. Each segment evaluates through the
    // CubicBezier2D / CubicBezier3D Eval in `library CurvesShapes`.

    // The point on a chain of cubic Bezier segments at t.
    Eval(self: CompositeBezier2D, t: Number): Point2D
    {
        var n = self.Segments.Count;
        var i = (t * n.ToNumber).Floor.ToInteger.Clamp(0, n - 1);
        return self.Segments[i].Eval(t * n.ToNumber - i.ToNumber);
    }

    // The point on a chain of cubic Bezier segments at t.
    Eval(self: CompositeBezier3D, t: Number): Point3D
    {
        var n = self.Segments.Count;
        var i = (t * n.ToNumber).Floor.ToInteger.Clamp(0, n - 1);
        return self.Segments[i].Eval(t * n.ToNumber - i.ToNumber);
    }

    //==
    // # Knot vectors and B-spline / NURBS domains
    //
    // The readers for the knot-vector curves declared in `splines.types.plato`:
    // knot count and lookup, the parameter domain a given degree covers, and the
    // de-homogenized (weighted) control point that a Cox-de Boor evaluator would
    // consume. Cox-de Boor evaluation itself is not shipped — see the note below.

    //==
    // # B-splines and NURBS
    //
    // Evaluation is the Cox-de Boor RECURRENCE on the basis functions, not the
    // de Boor triangular algorithm. Both compute the same curve; the recurrence
    // is an ordinary recursive function over (index, degree), which this
    // vocabulary expresses directly, where the triangular form wants a carried
    // per-level array it cannot spell. The recurrence recomputes shared
    // subterms, so the cost is exponential in the DEGREE — fine at cubic, and
    // the reason a tessellation loop should substitute de Boor.
    // https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Boor%27s_algorithm

    // The number of knots in a knot vector. For a curve with N control points
    // of degree D this must equal N + D + 1.
    Count(self: KnotVector): Integer
        => self.Knots.Count;

    // The knot at the given position.
    KnotAt(self: KnotVector, index: Integer): Number
        => self.Knots[index];

    // The parameter domain a B-spline of the given degree covers: knots
    // [Degree, Count - Degree - 1]. Outside it the basis is not a partition of
    // unity. Precondition: the knot count matches the degree and point count.
    Domain(self: KnotVector, degree: Integer): NumberInterval
        => (self.KnotAt(degree), self.KnotAt(self.Count - degree - 1));

    // The domain of a plane B-spline: its knot vector restricted by its degree.
    ParameterDomain(self: BSplineCurve2D): NumberInterval
        => self.Knots.Domain(self.Degree);

    // The domain of a space B-spline: its knot vector restricted by its degree.
    ParameterDomain(self: BSplineCurve3D): NumberInterval
        => self.Knots.Domain(self.Degree);

    // The domain of a plane NURBS curve.
    ParameterDomain(self: NurbsCurve2D): NumberInterval
        => self.Knots.Domain(self.Degree);

    // The domain of a space NURBS curve.
    ParameterDomain(self: NurbsCurve3D): NumberInterval
        => self.Knots.Domain(self.Degree);

    // The de-homogenized control point of a NURBS curve: the control point
    // scaled by its weight, the form Cox-de Boor consumes.
    WeightedControlPoint(self: NurbsCurve2D, index: Integer): Vector2D
        => self.ControlPoints[index].PositionVector * self.Weights[index];
```
